Getting data into Microsoft Foundry
Generative AI comes idx_caaf94ad with several skills that enrich an application with just a few interactions
or prompts. The same situation happens with agents, where an LLM is part of the core, and it
can make it functional. However, when it is necessary to manage a deeper level of knowledge
in a specific context, for example, your own business model, data becomes relevant.
When we bring together AI and data, we are enabling our AI applications the possibility of
leveraging all out-of-the-box LLM skills with the highest level of business or specific
knowledge based on our own information.
Microsoft Foundry idx_67ae52b7 comes with different options to work with data according to the
requirements we need to solve. From connecting with real-time data, transactional sources,
and online services to static data, Microsoft Foundry can cover many of these scenarios to give

Azure AI Search
Microsoft Foundry idx_bb5a60ba has a close integration with Azure AI Search for idx_d1c6fd8e expanding the possibilities
to interact with data. Azure AI Search is an Azure service for indexing and querying different
types of data stored in other services connected to Azure AI Search. It allows different types of
services as sources for indexing content, such as Storage Accounts, Cosmos DB databases, SQL
Database, through Logic Apps connectors, among others.
Connect Azure AI Search by navigating to Operate, then Admin, and clicking on Add

Figure 3.3: Connecting to an Azure AI Search instance
Model Context Protocol
While the idx_6c2fea06 usage of Generative AI has increased for creating a new generation of applications,
more data scenarios are coming to the top of idx_d4fb2b84 requirements. Model Context Protocol or MCP is
an open standard for standardizing how AI systems interact with each other, especially LLMs.
With standardized connectivity, MCP allows AI models to interact with various data sources
through a single protocol.
Microsoft Foundry allows connections with MCP servers, so you can take advantage of the data
that comes from it for your AI project. There are different types of connections for the servers
available in the Tools catalog. This depends on how the server is hosted.
Once an MCP server is connected, it can expose tools that agents and AI applications can use
during execution. These tools can help the application retrieve information, call external
systems, or perform specific actions based on the user's request. For example, an agent could
53 Working with Data
use an MCP-connected tool to look up customer information, query a product catalog, check a
support ticket, retrieve data from a database, or interact with another business system.
MCP is useful idx_859831d3 when your AI application needs access to live or idx_829e4081 frequently changing data.
Instead of copying all the data into the model or adding large amounts of context to every
prompt, the agent can call the connected MCP tool only when needed. This keeps the
application more flexible and makes it easier to work with systems that are updated regularly.
It is also important to understand that MCP does not replace storage accounts or Azure AI
Search. Storage accounts are useful for storing files and datasets, while Azure AI Search is
useful for indexing and retrieving content for search-based scenarios. MCP supports a different
pattern: connecting the AI application to external tools and systems so it can retrieve data or
perform actions dynamically during a conversation or workflow.
With these options in mind, Microsoft Foundry gives you several ways to bring data into an AI

project. You can connect static files through storage, searchable content through Azure AI
Search, and live tools or external systems through MCP. Now that we have reviewed these data
connection options, let's look at one of the most common patterns for using data with
generative AI: Retrieval-Augmented Generation or RAG.
Exploring the RAG pattern
In Microsoft Foundry, data is idx_27fb0a99 central to Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) patterns.
The better your data, the better your AI responses. RAG solves a critical limitation: standard
LLMs have a knowledge cutoff and can hallucinate when they don't know something. By
connecting your proprietary data to an LLM via RAG, you get accurate, up-to-date answers
grounded in your actual information.
To effectively harness the power of data in AI projects, various patterns can be employed, one
of which is the RAG model. RAG combines the strengths of retrieval-based and generation-
based approaches, allowing AI systems to access and utilize vast amounts of external
information idx_b91535d4 dynamically. This combination enhances the model's ability to generate more
accurate and contextually relevant responses by retrieving pertinent data from a large corpus
before generating the final output. Such hybrid models are particularly useful in applications
requiring up-to-date information and nuanced understanding, such as customer support,
content creation, and research.
To understand more about RAG, let's see the following figure:

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 54
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 54
Figure 3.4: How the RAG pattern works
Let's explain idx_48b2be12 this process:
Step 1 - Data Sources: Gather all your knowledge (documents, PDFs, specs, FAQs) that
the system will use
Step 2 - Embedding Process: Convert text into mathematical vectors so the system
can understand meaning and search fast
Step 3 - Vector Index: Store all vectors in Azure AI Search as a searchable, semantic
knowledge base
Step 4 - User Query: User asks a natural question (e.g., " What's the best EV for
cold climates?")
Step 5 - Vector Search: Find the 3-5 most relevant documents from your knowledge
base using semantic similarity
Step 6 - Context Window: Format the retrieved documents and insert them into the
prompt with the user's question
Step 7 - LLM Generation: LLM reads the question + context and generates an accurate,
synthesized response
Step 8 - Grounded Output: Return answer to user, traceable to source documents (not
a hallucination)

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: 7.8 55 Working with Data
chunks.content:
7.8 55 Working with Data
Choosing RAG idx_c1211122 over other patterns depends on the specific needs and goals of your AI
application. Here are some reasons why RAG might be idx_2509c190 preferred:
Access to Up-to-Date Information: RAG can dynamically retrieve the latest
information from a large corpus, making it ideal for applications that require current
and contextually relevant data, such as customer support or real-time content
generation.
Enhanced Contextual Understanding: By combining retrieval and generation, RAG
can provide more accurate and contextually appropriate responses. This is particularly
useful in complex queries where the model needs to understand and integrate diverse
pieces of information.
Scalability: RAG can handle vast amounts of data efficiently, as it retrieves only the
most relevant information needed for generating responses. This makes it scalable for
large-scale applications.
Flexibility: RAG idx_6d04d93c can be adapted to various domains and tasks by simply changing the
retrieval of the response. This flexibility allows it to be used in a wide range of
applications without extensive retraining.
Improved Performance: In scenarios where the generation model alone might
struggle to provide accurate answers, the retrieval component can significantly boost
performance by supplying pertinent information that the generation model can build
upon.
Now that we understand how the RAG pattern works and why it is useful, let's ground the
concept in a practical example. The next section compares a traditional API-based customer
support workflow with a RAG-based approach in Microsoft Foundry, showing how the
architecture, response flow, maintenance effort, and cost profile can change when knowledge
retrieval is handled through an indexed knowledge base.
Real-world example and cost implications
Let's ground RAG in a idx_54035204 practical scenario. Imagine a customer service system for an electric
vehicle manufacturer that needs to answer questions about vehicle specifications, warranty
information, and local charging stations.
•
•
•
•
•

chunks.heading: Chapter 3 56
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 56
Without RAG (Traditional approach)
A company would typically implement this using two separate systems:
API-based system: Query a traditional REST API for vehicle specifications and
warranty information. The API calls would be made for each customer query, with data
being sent over the network.
Web scraping or scheduled batch jobs: Pull charging station data from external
services every night and store it in a database.
The workflow would look as follows:
Receive the customer question
Call the required API
Wait for the API response
Search the database for relevant information
Format the results
Send the response to the customer
Now, here idx_b2ef51e0 is what it costs with traditional APIs:
API calls: $0.002 per request (typical for enterprise APIs) × 10,000 requests/month =
$20/month
Database maintenance: $50/month (storage, indexing, updates)
Data refresh jobs: 1 batch job per night × $5/month = $5/month
Human maintenance: 5-10 hours/month for updates and issues = $200-$400/month
Latency issues during peak hours requiring infrastructure scaling: +$100-$200/
month
Total monthly cost: $375-$675
With RAG in Microsoft Foundry
The same system uses a single unified approach: Index vehicle specs, warranty info, and
charging data once in Azure AI Search. The LLM retrieves relevant information from the index
and generates a natural, conversational response.
The workflow becomes:
Receive the customer question
Access the relevant knowledge base through the LLM
Generate a response based on the retrieved information
Send the response to the customer
•
•

chunks.content:
4.57 Working with Data
Now, let's look idx_a6945579 at the costs with RAG:
Azure AI Search: $50/month (Standard tier, handles millions of documents)
Embedding model: $0.00005 per 1K tokens for text-embedding-3-small (typically
$2-3/month)
LLM inference: $0.01 per 1K completion tokens (about $15-25/month for 10,000
queries)
Storage: Already included in AI Search ($50)
Initial data indexing: One-time cost (included in setup)
Total monthly cost: $65–80
But there are more benefits beyond cost, such as:
Faster Response Times: RAG typically responds in 500-800ms vs 1-2 seconds with API
chains due to fewer network round-trips.
Better Context Understanding: The LLM can synthesize multiple pieces of
information from the knowledge base into a single coherent answer, something APIs
alone cannot do well.
Reduced Maintenance Burden: No need for custom integration code between APIs,
rate limiting logic, or error handling for individual services.
Scalability Without Scaling Infrastructure: As query volume grows, you don't need
to provision additional servers; Azure AI Search and LLMs handle auto-scaling
transparently.
Flexibility for Changes: To add new data sources, you simply add them to the
knowledge base. With traditional APIs, you'd need to modify integration code.
This is where idx_d4d1e213 RAG truly shines. It's not just cheaper; it's faster to implement, easier to
maintain, and scales better than traditional API-based approaches.
When to use RAG vs. Traditional APIs
Not every idx_49e7ddd5 scenario benefits from RAG. Here's a practical guide to help you decide:
Use RAG When:
You have a large corpus of static or semi-static data (documentation, knowledge bases,
product specifications). Example: 500+ pages of technical documentation that
customers query frequently
You need contextual synthesis (combining multiple data sources into one coherent
answer). Example: "What's the best electric vehicle for someone living in a cold

chunks.content:
Chapter 3 58
climate?" requires synthesizing vehicle specs, battery performance, and charging
infrastructure data.
Data changes infrequently (monthly or quarterly updates). Example: Product catalog,
technical documentation, policy guidelines.
You want to reduce API latency and infrastructure complexity. Example: Customer
support with response-time SLAs under 2 seconds.
Cost is a concern (especially at scale). Example: Processing 100,000+ queries/month
where API costs become prohibitive.
You need to maintain conversation context over multiple turns. Example: A chat
interface where the AI needs to remember earlier points in the conversation.
Do NOT Use RAG When:
You need real-time data that changes by the second. Example: Stock prices, live
inventory counts, real-time weather updates. Use traditional APIs that give you the
latest data.
Data is too large to practically index (multi-terabyte datasets). Example: Complete
scientific literature (billions of papers). Consider federated approaches or smaller,
curated subsets.
Your queries are simple and don't need context synthesis. Example: " What is the
price of product ABC? " — a simple database lookup is faster.
You idx_001a041b need frequent real-time updates (within seconds or minutes). Example: Stock
trading platforms, real-time traffic monitoring. RAG indexing latency (typically 5–30
minutes) is too slow.
Your data is already accessible via well-maintained, fast APIs. Example: Using Stripe
API for payment data, Salesforce API for CRM data. Maintain the API integration; RAG
adds unnecessary complexity.
Security/compliance requires immediate data deletion. Example: GDPR right-to-be-
forgotten requirements. RAG indexing creates copies of data, making immediate
deletion complex.
In practice, many successful systems use both RAG and APIs:
Use RAG for historical, reference data (policies, documentation, specifications)
Use APIs for real-time data (inventory, pricing, user-specific information)
Combine them in the LLM prompt: " Based on our product docs AND the current
inventory data."

Let's look at an example. An e-commerce support agent might:
Use RAG to access product specs and return policies (static, changed monthly)
Call a REST API to check real-time inventory (changes by the minute)
Combine both in the response: " This phone costs $799 (from our price API) and
comes with a 2 ‑ year warranty (from our policies, retrieved via RAG)"
This hybrid approach gives you the best of both worlds: freshness from APIs, cost-efficiency,
and context from RAG.
While other patterns idx_1dd45418 like Transformer models, GANs, or Federated Learning have their own
strengths and are suited for different types of tasks, RAG's unique combination of retrieval and
generation makes it particularly powerful for applications requiring real-time, contextually

rich responses. Let's have a look at some of the other available patterns.
Looking at some other AI architecture patterns
In addition to RAG, there idx_f202c62c are several other architectural patterns that can be employed to
enhance AI applications. These patterns help in addressing various challenges such as data
integration, model efficiency, and real-time processing, thereby enabling more robust and
versatile AI solutions.
Here are some notable patterns with analogies to better understand:
Transformer Models: Imagine idx_286b99a5 you have a book, and idx_3322b26a you want to understand the
meaning of each sentence. Transformer models are like super-smart readers that can
look at the entire book at once and understand the context of each word. They are great
at tasks like translating languages or summarizing text because they can see the big
picture and the details at the same time.
Federated Learning: Think of federated learning as a group project where everyone
idx_7d7b4b90 works on their own part at home but shares their progress with the group. Instead of
sending all the data to one place, each person's device learns from its own data and
then sends only the learning updates to a central place. This way, your data stays
private, but the group still learns together.
Autoencoders: They idx_cf7475c7 are like artists who idx_05bccf16 can draw a picture and then recreate it from
memory. They take an input (like an image), compress it into a simpler form, and then
try to recreate the original image from this compressed version. This helps in reducing
noise or finding important features in the data.
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs): Imagine two artists in a friendly
competition: one idx_f42c3ba6 tries idx_afcad510 to create realistic paintings, and the other tries to spot the fakes.
The first artist gets better at making realistic paintings, and the second gets better at
•
•
•
•
•
•
•

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 3 60
chunks.content:
Chapter 3 60
spotting fakes. GANs work similarly, with one part creating data (like images) and the
other part trying to detect if it's real or fake. This helps in generating very realistic
images or data.
Reinforcement Learning: Think idx_23c9fe91 of a video idx_d5061b3b game where a character learns to play by
trying different actions and getting points for good moves. Reinforcement learning is
like this: an AI learns by doing actions and getting rewards or penalties. Over time, it
learns the best actions to maximize its rewards, just like a gamer getting better at a
game.
Graph Neural Networks (GNNs): Imagine a idx_ccab7ccd social idx_69b98563 network where each person is a
node, and their friendships are connected between nodes. GNNs are like super-smart
analysts who can understand complex relationships in such networks. They are great
for tasks where relationships and connections matter, like predicting how diseases
spread or recommending friends on social media.
Transfer Learning: Think idx_69f2ffb8 of transfer learning as a student who has learned math and
now uses that knowledge to learn physics faster. In AI, transfer learning means taking a
model trained on one task and using it as a starting point for a different but related

Choosing the Right Model
We've been thoroughly learning more about the extensive capabilities that Microsoft Foundry

deployment process for AI models. Now, it's crucial to actively engage with the AI model to
evaluate and identify the one that perfectly aligns with our project's specific needs and goals.
This step will ensure we leverage the most suitable model for optimal results.
In this chapter, you will learn how to choose the most appropriate model from the Model
catalog for your needs. Furthermore, we will provide step-by-step instructions on how to
implement the selected model into your AI application, ensuring you can maximize its
potential.
By the end of this chapter, we will gain a better understanding of how to choose an AI model
based on various needs and variables, compare the performance of one model against others,
deploy a selected model from the Microsoft Foundry portal for use in a project, and test the

Model differences and data governance implications
When selecting an AI model, it is not enough to compare only benchmark scores, response
quality, or cost. Different models make different trade-offs in how they process data, where
they run, how much context they can handle, how predictable their outputs are, and what
compliance controls they support. These differences can directly affect whether a model is
appropriate for your organization's data governance requirements.
In this section, we will look at the idx_cf484c5f main governance-related factors you should review before
choosing a model. These include model architecture, data residency, context window size,
knowledge cutoff, output reproducibility, fine-tuning, data ownership, safety behavior, and
regulatory alignment. By the end of this section, you should be able to evaluate a model not
only by how well it performs, but also by whether it fits your security, compliance, and
operational requirements.
Model architecture differences
Where is idx_9236bff8 your data processed? Cloud-based models (Azure OpenAI, Mistral) process data on
provider servers, while self-hosted models (open-source) keep data in your infrastructure.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 72
chunks.content:
Azure OpenAI models handle complex reasoning tasks on Microsoft servers. Meta's Llama
models prioritize efficiency and can run locally. Open-source models give you complete control
over data residency. The key governance difference is that with cloud models, you trust the
provider's data handling, while with self-hosted models, you control everything.
Impact: Cloud models are convenient but require trusting the provider. Self-hosted models
offer control but need infrastructure investment. Choose based on your data residency
requirements and compliance needs.
Context window and token limits
How idx_c4cefcda much data can the model process at once? GPT-5.2 handles 128,000 tokens per request.
Smaller models handle between 4,000 and 8,000 tokens, requiring you to split documents.
Larger context windows let you process complete documents as units. Smaller windows
require fragmented data, creating consistency challenges: how do you ensure split documents
maintain coherence across multiple requests?
Impact: Large context windows simplify data handling but transmit more sensitive
information per request. Small windows fragment data but limit exposure. For regulated data,
small windows may be preferable; for efficiency, larger windows work better.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 74
chunks.content:
Chapter 4 74
Training data and knowledge cutoff
What idx_4b66f6be does the model already know? GPT-5.2 was trained through idx_2c3ad63a early 2025. Older models
have 2023-2024 cutoffs. This affects what you must provide through RAG.
If your policies changed after the model's training date, the model's knowledge may contradict
idx_ad486fc8 your current rules. This isn't just a user experience issue—it's a idx_7d5fc064 compliance problem. Your
model might confidently give customers outdated information.
Impact: Always document your model's knowledge cutoff date. Use RAG to inject current
information. Implement version control of your knowledge base to track what information was
used when—critical for compliance audits.
Output determinism and reproducibility
Are idx_be79c6ce model responses consistent? Temperature settings control this. Lower temperature (0.1)
produces predictable outputs; higher temperature (0.9) produces varied, creative responses.
Compliance work, healthcare, and idx_88fec769 financial applications need reproducible outputs for audit
purposes. If regulators ask, "Why did the model make this decision?", you need to reproduce
that exact output. High randomness with sensitive data creates audit trails you can't defend.
Impact: Regulated industries and sensitive data require low temperature settings. This isn't
optional—it's a compliance requirement. Document your temperature settings as part of your
governance evidence.
Fine-Tuning capabilities and data ownership
Can you customize idx_0c27b5bd the model with your data? Some models idx_d03ba490 support fine-tuning; others don't.
When you fine-tune, you share training examples with the provider.
Critical questions: Does the provider keep your data? Can it improve the base model? Are your
proprietary examples protected? Microsoft Foundry lets you specify data retention policies, but
these vary by model. Highly sensitive data (healthcare, finance, PII) need careful fine-tuning
decisions.
Impact: Understand exactly what happens to your training data before fine-tuning. For
sensitive data, prefer RAG (inject knowledge via knowledge base) instead of training it into the
model. This keeps your data completely separate from the model's permanent parameters.
Safety and moderation guardrails
How idx_dc44c20b does the model handle sensitive requests? Different models refuse different things. Some
aggressively block perceived harmful requests; others are more permissive.
75 Choosing the Right Model
A model too aggressive at refusal blocks legitimate business requests. A model too permissive
might process PII unsafely. Your data governance policy needs to account for each model's
baseline safety posture.
Impact: Document each model's baseline safety features. For sensitive customer data, prefer
models with stronger built-in safety. If using a permissive model, compensate with more

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 74
chunks.content:
sophisticated guardrails. Include this documentation in your compliance evidence.
Regulatory and compliance alignment
Does the idx_54508598 model meet legal requirements? Some models are HIPAA-certified, some are GDPR-
compliant (EU data centers), and some are FedRAMP-approved. These aren't guidelines—
they're legal requirements.
Processing EU data with a US-only model violates GDPR. Healthcare work requires HIPAA
certification. US government work requires FedRAMP. Open-source models can be self-hosted
to meet data residency requirements that cloud models can't.
Impact: First filter models by legal compliance. Eliminate any model that doesn't meet your
regulatory requirements, regardless of performance. Only after compliance filtering should you
evaluate performance and cost.
After reviewing idx_78476df3 the governance implications of model architecture, context windows, training
data, reproducibility, fine-tuning, safety behavior, and regulatory alignment, the next step is to
turn those considerations into practical selection checks. Microsoft Foundry gives you several
places to review this information, but you still need a clear set of questions to guide the
decision before choosing a model.
How to address these governance challenges in Microsoft
Foundry
Choosing idx_3b9194ba a model responsibly means converting governance concerns into concrete review
criteria. In Microsoft Foundry, you should not evaluate a model only by how well it performs
on a task. You should also check whether it satisfies your requirements for data residency,
retention, auditability, version control, PII protection, and compliance. The following
questions can be used as a practical checklist when reviewing models in the Catalog, Model
Leaderboards, or Compare models section:
Data Residency: Does data remain in your infrastructure or go to the provider? Do
regulations require data residency (GDPR, local laws)?
Data Retention: Does the provider keep data after processing? Check Microsoft's data
handling policies for each model.

improve the base model? Check model-specific policies.
Auditability: Can you trace which knowledge base documents influenced responses?
Can you reproduce outputs for audits? (RAG + low temperature helps.)
PII Protection: Does the model detect PII? Can guardrails block PII in outputs?
(Essential for compliance work.)
Version Control: Can you lock to specific model versions? Do updates change response
behavior? (Critical for regulatory defense.)
Governance idx_c40e8fdc considerations matter as much as performance metrics. A high-performing model
that violates compliance is unusable. A slightly lower-performing model that meets

Chapter 4 80
Latency vs performance trade-offs
When idx_cfcc3e60 selecting a model, you face a classic trade-off: faster responses (low latency) or better
quality answers (high performance). Understanding this trade-off is essential for choosing the
right model for your specific use case.
The core trade-off
Larger, more idx_4c91f5b5 capable models (GPT-5.2, Claude Opus) produce higher quality responses but
take longer to generate answers—typically 2-5 seconds per response. Smaller, more efficient
models (Claude Haiku, Mistral) respond in milliseconds but sacrifice some quality and
reasoning capability. This difference compounds at scale: if you serve 1,000 concurrent users,
latency becomes a critical factor.
Your choice depends on your use case. Customer-facing chatbots prioritize latency—users
expect responses in under 2 seconds, or they perceive the system as slow and unresponsive.
Background batch processing jobs can tolerate longer latency if responses are higher quality.
Real-time applications (customer support chat, live text input) need fast models. Research
applications can wait for better answers.
Making the trade-off decision
Start by idx_4ea9718b defining your latency requirement. What's acceptable for your users? Then evaluate
model options that meet that threshold. If you need sub-2-second response times, some high-
performance models are eliminated immediately. If you can tolerate 5-second responses, you
have more options. The Model Leaderboards show Throughput (tokens/sec) metrics—use
these to estimate response time based on your typical query length.
Remember, paying for a high-performance model that's too slow for your use case is money
wasted. Conversely, choosing a faster model that doesn't meet quality standards will degrade
user experience. The right model balances both dimensions for your specific requirements.
After considering latency and performance, the next decision is how much you need to
customize the model's behavior. In many cases, the base model may already be capable
enough, but you still need to guide it toward the right tone, format, or task behavior. This is
where you need to decide whether prompt engineering is sufficient or whether fine-tuning is
justified.
Fine-tuning vs. prompt engineering: Which should you
choose?
Microsoft Foundry offers two primary strategies for customizing models:
Fine-tuning: Training the model on your data
Prompt engineering: Crafting better instructions
•
•
81 Choosing the Right Model
Each has distinct trade-offs regarding cost, speed, and effectiveness.
Prompt engineering
Prompt engineering, i.e., writing idx_e4b6d329 better instructions and providing examples, is your first
choice. It's fast, requires no training time, and often solves customization needs without extra
cost. A well-engineered prompt can dramatically improve model behavior for specific tasks.

chunks.title: microsoftfoundryinaction
chunks.heading: Chapter 4 80
chunks.content:
Start with clear instructions. Describe exactly what you want the model to do, provide
examples of good outputs, specify the format of responses, and clarify edge cases. Add a few-
shot examples (2-3 examples of input/output pairs) to show the model the pattern you want.
Test iteratively and refine. Many customization problems are solved this way without touching
fine-tuning.
Prompt engineering is idx_1d81218b ideal for the following:
Style customization: You can use prompt engineering to control whether the response
should sound formal, casual, concise, friendly, or technical
Output format specifications: You can define the structure of the response, such as
JSON, CSV, bullet points, tables, or structured text
Task-specific behavior: You can guide the model to follow specific rules for tasks such
as summarization, translation, classification, or content rewriting
Reasoning guidance: You can instruct the model to follow a step-by-step approach
when solving problems or explaining complex topics
Prompt engineering should usually be your first customization approach because it is fast,
low-cost, and often effective for controlling tone, format, task behavior, and reasoning style
without retraining the model.
Fine-tuning
Fine-tuning makes idx_d72d48b9 sense when prompt engineering alone can't achieve your goals. Fine-
tuning trains the model on your specific data, making it an "expert" in your domain. A model
fine-tuned on your customer support conversations learns your company's tone, your common
issues, and your resolution patterns.
Fine-tuning comes with several costs:
Training time: This can range from a few minutes to several hours, depending on the
size of the dataset
GPU resources: Training may require paid compute resources

should look like
Ongoing maintenance: The fine-tuned model may need to be retrained when your
data, requirements, or expected outputs change

Table 4.1: Choosing between prompt engineering and fine-tuning based on customization needs
Prompt engineering is usually the more cost-effective option because it does not require
additional compute resources and can often be improved within a few hours of iteration. Fine-
tuning, on the other hand, requires paid compute resources, a training pipeline, prepared
datasets, and additional time for testing and maintenance. If the problem can be solved with a
few hours of prompt engineering, the return on investment is usually clear. However, if you

worth comparing the time required for prompt engineering with the compute and
maintenance costs of fine-tuning before deciding which approach to use.

Working with Workflows
In the previous chapter, we focused on choosing the right model and deploying it inside
Microsoft Foundry. We discussed how to evaluate model capabilities, configure deployments,
and make them available for real use. By that point, you had something powerful in your
hands: a deployed large language model ready to generate responses. But as we hinted before,
a deployed model alone does not make a complete AI solution.
Once a model is running, the real challenge begins. How do you control what it does? How do
you ensure responses follow business rules? How do you add decision logic, integrate external
systems, or escalate sensitive cases to a human reviewer? This is where interaction design
becomes essential. Enterprise AI is rarely a single prompt and a single response. It's a
structured process — one that may include classification, validation, branching, tool calls, and
formatting before a final answer is returned. In Microsoft Foundry, this orchestration layer is
implemented using Workflows.
Workflows allow you to visually design how your AI system behaves. Instead of embedding all
logic inside a single prompt, you break it into clear steps connected in a controlled execution
path. This approach improves reliability, maintainability, and transparency—especially in
production environments where traceability and governance matter.
In this chapter, we'll explore how to design AI interaction logic using Workflows in the new
Microsoft Foundry portal. You'll learn how to create workflows from scratch, connect model
nodes, implement conditional logic, integrate tools, enforce structured outputs, and test

deployment into a structured, enterprise-ready AI workflow that is reliable, extensible, and
ready to power real-world solutions.

AI interaction design in Microsoft Foundry
We have focused so far idx_6c64c0e6 on choosing and deploying the right idx_0e4d2623 model. By now, you should have at
least one model deployment ready inside your Microsoft Foundry project. But here's the
reality: deploying a model is only the starting point. A model can generate text while a
workflow defines how that text is generated.
That distinction is critical. In real-world enterprise solutions, AI is rarely a single prompt sent
to a single model. Instead, it's a sequence of decisions: classify the request, retrieve context,
validate risk, apply business rules, and only then generate a response. This orchestration layer
is exactly what Workflows in Microsoft Foundry are designed to handle.
Where Workflows fit in the portal
Inside a Microsoft Foundry Project, Workflows idx_49d59cfe live under the Build section. They idx_d8efff09 allow you to
visually design the execution logic of your AI solution using a node-based canvas.
Think of it this way:
Model: Generates content
Workflow: Defines the logic
Agent: Exposes the experience
When you open the portal and navigate to your project, you'll find Workflows as a first-class
building block for designing AI behavior beyond simple prompt-response interactions.

Understanding workflows
Up to this point, we've idx_00e7ee4d talked about why orchestration matters. We've seen that a model
deployment alone does not define behavior — it simply provides capability. The real
intelligence of an enterprise AI solution comes from how that capability is structured,
controlled, and connected to business logic. That structure is what Workflows brings to
Microsoft Foundry.
When organizations move from experimentation to production, they quickly realize something
important: prompts grow messy. Teams start adding instructions like "if the user says X, do Y"
or "if risk is high, escalate" directly inside a single prompt. At first, this works. But as
complexity increases, maintainability decreases. Debugging becomes difficult. Auditing
becomes unclear. Small changes introduce unexpected behavior.
Workflows solve this by separating logic into explicit, visual steps. Instead of hiding
orchestration inside a long prompt, you define:
What comes first
What depends on what?
Where decisions are made
When humans are involved
How outputs are structured
This shift — from prompt-centric thinking to workflow-centric design — is what transforms
generative AI from a demo into a reliable system. Now let's open the canvas and understand
how this works in practice.
When you create a new workflow from Workflows, Microsoft Foundry offers predefined
workflow patterns that idx_44be2744 reflect common enterprise scenarios. These templates are not rigid
structures—they are starting points designed to accelerate implementation while maintaining
best practices.
